chapter: Life in New York in the 1940s
title: Ray Nance's dancing and shining his horn
summary: Edison says Ray Nance's dancing and singing kept him active and distracted from drugs.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: You know whom we haven't really remarkable, mentioned who was and that was Ray Nance.
Now, I mean, he carried on all that time and he even used to do that dance with that kick too.
Yeah. Well, you see, that kept him going because he was perspiring.
You see, he was active. He was active.
And he had something to deviate his mind from the drugs to dancing. And he got his exercise.

And, you know, you take the Charlie Parkers and the Fats Navarros and the guys like that, they sat down and they played. Well, Ray Nance, you know, he would get up, he would do his dance, he would sing, you know.
But another thing about him, you never saw him nodding off. Not like --

Well, he used to keep his horn so clean. You know, every night, he'd shine his horn constantly. Then he would find himself getting ready to nod, he'd drag his horn -- he had the cleanest horn in the world, you see. Remember when he used to take and shine his horn all the time? You understand?
Well, even -- Ray was a very intelligent man, really, you know. It's just that he got caught up in that.
Oh, it's just so bad. You know, all the good ones, they look like they're just leaving, for some reason or other, than just natural causes.
Well, you know, it's a rough profession even without something like that, isn't it.
